nodes.summary: For a key $x$ and a binary tree $t$ over a linearly ordered type, the tree component of the access of $x$ in $t$ is the tree obtained by splaying $x$ in $t$.
nodes.title: The tree returned by a splay-tree access

nodes.summary: For a key $x$ and a binary tree $t$ over a linearly ordered type, the access of $x$ in $t$ is the pair $(b, t')$, where $t'$ is the tree obtained by splaying $x$ in $t$ and $b$ is true exactly when $t'$ is nonempty and its root key is $x$.
nodes.title: Splay-tree access

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be an ordered binary tree over a linearly ordered type and let $x$ be a key. When $t$ is split at $x$, every key of the left part is strictly less than $x$ and every key of the right part is strictly greater than $x$.
nodes.title: Splitting an ordered tree separates the keys around the split key

nodes.summary: For an ordered binary tree $t$ over a linearly ordered type and a key $x$, the splay-tree membership test of $x$ in $t$ returns true if and only if $x$ is a key of $t$.
nodes.title: Correctness of the splay-tree membership test

nodes.summary: For a key $x$ and a binary tree $t$ over a linearly ordered type, the membership test of $x$ in $t$ is the Boolean component of the access of $x$ in $t$: it is true exactly when the tree obtained by splaying $x$ in $t$ is nonempty and its root key is $x$.
nodes.title: Splay-tree membership test

nodes.summary: For every key $x$ and every binary tree $t$ over a linearly ordered type, the inorder traversal of the tree obtained by splaying $x$ in $t$ equals the inorder traversal of $t$. No search-tree ordering of $t$ is assumed.
nodes.title: Splaying preserves the inorder traversal

nodes.summary: For a key $x$ and a binary tree $t$ over a linearly ordered type, inserting $x$ into $t$ splays $x$ in $t$, splits the resulting tree at $x$ into a left part and a right part, and returns the tree whose root key is $x$, whose left subtree is the left part and whose right subtree is the right part.
nodes.title: Splay-tree insertion

nodes.summary: For keys $x$ and $y$ and a binary tree $t$ over a linearly ordered type, $y$ is a key of the tree obtained by splay-tree insertion of $x$ into $t$ if and only if $y = x$ or $y$ is a key of $t$.
nodes.title: Keys after splay-tree insertion

nodes.summary: For keys $x$ and $y$ and a binary tree $t$ over a linearly ordered type, if $y$ is a key of the left part or of the right part of the split of $t$ at $x$, then $y$ is a key of $t$.
nodes.title: Splay-tree split parts contain only original keys

nodes.summary: For keys $x$ and $y$ and a binary tree $t$ over a linearly ordered type, $y$ is a key of the tree obtained by splaying $x$ in $t$ if and only if $y$ is a key of $t$.
nodes.title: Splaying preserves membership

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a binary tree with keys in a linearly ordered type, and let $x$ and $y$ be keys with $y \ne x$. If $y$ occurs as a key of $t$, then $y$ occurs as a key of the left part or of the right part of the split of $t$ at $x$. The tree $t$ need not be a binary search tree.
nodes.title: Keys other than the split key survive a split

nodes.summary: For every binary tree $t$ with keys in a linearly ordered type and every key $x$, the tree obtained by splaying $x$ in $t$ has the same number of nodes as $t$.
nodes.title: Splaying preserves the number of nodes

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a binary tree with keys in a linearly ordered type and let $x$ be a key. If $t$ is a binary search tree (at every node, every key of the left subtree is strictly smaller and every key of the right subtree strictly larger than the key of the node), then the splay-tree insertion of $x$ into $t$ is again a binary search tree.
nodes.title: Splay-tree insertion preserves the search-tree property

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a binary tree with keys in a linearly ordered type and let $x$ be a key. If $t$ is a binary search tree (at every node, every key of the left subtree is strictly smaller and every key of the right subtree strictly larger than the key of the node), then the tree obtained by splaying $x$ in $t$ is again a binary search tree.
nodes.title: Splaying preserves the search-tree property

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a binary tree with keys in a linearly ordered type and let $x$ be a key. If $t$ is a binary search tree (at every node, every key of the left subtree is strictly smaller and every key of the right subtree strictly larger than the key of the node), then the left part and the right part of the split of $t$ at $x$ are both binary search trees.
nodes.title: Both parts of a split search tree are search trees

nodes.summary: For every binary tree $t$ with keys in a linearly ordered type and every key $x$, the splay-tree insertion of $x$ into $t$ is a nonempty tree whose root key is $x$.
nodes.title: Splay-tree insertion puts the inserted key at the root

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a binary search tree with keys in a linearly ordered type (at every node, every key of the left subtree is strictly smaller and every key of the right subtree strictly larger than the key of the node), and let $x$ be a key that occurs in $t$. Then the tree obtained by splaying $x$ in $t$ is nonempty and its root key is $x$.
nodes.title: Root key after splaying a present key

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a binary search tree with keys in a linearly ordered type (at every node, every key of the left subtree is strictly smaller and every key of the right subtree strictly larger than the key of the node), and let $x$ be a key that occurs in $t$. Then there are binary trees $l$ and $r$ such that splaying $x$ in $t$ gives the tree whose root holds $x$, with left subtree $l$ and right subtree $r$.
nodes.title: Splaying a present key brings it to the root

nodes.summary: The optional root key of a binary tree is undefined (none) for the empty tree, and is the key $k$ for a tree whose root node holds $k$.
nodes.title: Root key of a splay tree

nodes.summary: For every key $x$ of a linearly ordered type, splaying $x$ in the empty binary tree gives the empty tree.
nodes.title: Splaying the empty tree

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type and write $(k; L, R)$ for the binary tree with root key $k$, left subtree $L$ and right subtree $R$. For $x \in \alpha$, the splay $S_x(t)$ of a binary tree $t$ with keys in $\alpha$ is defined by recursion on $t$. The empty tree splays to itself, and $t = (k; L, R)$ is left unchanged if $x = k$, if $x < k$ and $L$ is empty, or if $x > k$ and $R$ is empty. If $x < k$ and…
nodes.title: Splay operation

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type, let $x \in \alpha$, and write $(k; L, R)$ for the binary tree with root key $k$, left subtree $L$ and right subtree $R$. The split of a binary tree with keys in $\alpha$ at $x$ is the pair of trees defined by recursion: the empty tree splits into two empty trees; if $x < k$ and $L$ splits into $(L_1, L_2)$, then $(k; L, R)$ splits into $(L_1, (k; L_2, R))$; if $k < x$ and…
nodes.title: Search-path split at a key
Computer Science

can_prove.label: ready to prove
can_prove.meaning: Statement is in Lean and nothing it needs is blocked, so the proof can start.

can_state.label: ready to state
can_state.meaning: Everything its statement uses is in Lean, so the statement can be written in Lean.

conditional.label: conditionally proved
conditional.meaning: Proof compiles, but rests on an open statement without a recorded Lean proof.

fully_proved.label: fully proved
fully_proved.meaning: Proved, and every prerequisite is fully proved too.

inventory_checked.label: inventory checked
inventory_checked.meaning: Module inventory checked in full; it records inspection, not a mathematical proof.

inventory_pending.label: inventory pending
inventory_pending.meaning: Module inventory not yet checked in full; it records inspection, not a mathematical proof.

not_ready.label: not ready
not_ready.meaning: Needs more blueprint work before it can be attempted.

proved.label: proved
proved.meaning: Proof compiles, but something it rests on is not finished.

stated.label: statement formalized
stated.meaning: Statement is in Lean; the proof is not.
